description:
We’re a team of italian master students combining hardware, AI and software expertise:

Nanotechnology engineering, for materials science and physical-systems thinking

Machine learning, from research to engineering

Software engineering, building fast, AI-assisted products

We’re interested in space exploration, planetary science and using NASA open data to solve real problems. We like challenges where physics, data and good software meet, especially work aimed towards space missions
summary:
POLENTA (Planetary Outcrop & Landing Environment Nearby Testbed Assistant) is a web tool that tells space companies and agencies where on Earth to test hardware for the Moon and Mars.
You pick a target site (three Artemis III candidate regions at the lunar South Pole, the Aristarchus Plateau, or the Phoenix and Gale landing sites on Mars) and a test: rover mobility, lidar landing hazard detection, or in-situ resource utilization. POLENTA scores every patch of bare land on Earth against that site with NASA data, measuring terrain the same way on both worlds (lunar slope, roughness and craters from LRO LOLA, computed with the same code as on NASADEM). Each test weighs the parameters differently, because the best analog depends on what you test.
For every place it shows how faithful the analogy is, where it breaks, and which indoor facilities cover what Earth can never reproduce, such as 1/6 gravity and vacuum.
Why it matters: teams keep going back to the same few famous sites, and choosing one takes weeks of desk study. POLENTA builds a ranked shortlist in minutes, and 61 of its 90 top places lie outside every known test site and analog region.
Demo deck: click or press → to advance.
details:
POLENTA (Planetary Outcrop & Landing Environment Nearby Testbed Assistant) tells space companies where on Earth to test hardware for the Moon and Mars, how faithful each place is, and what has to be tested indoors instead.

WHAT IT DOES

You pick a target site and a hardware test. Targets: Malapert Massif, Haworth and Nobile Rim 1 (Artemis III candidate regions at the lunar South Pole), the Aristarchus Plateau, and Phoenix and Gale on Mars. Tests: rover mobility, landing hazard detection with lidar, and in-situ resource utilization (ISRU). POLENTA ranks all the bare land on Earth that we have data for by how closely it reproduces that target for that test, in three views:

- Best on Earth: the most similar places anywhere.

- Unexplored: the same ranking without the well-studied analog regions and anything within 150 km of a known test site.

- Near you: the best places within 1,500, 3,000 or 5,000 km of the customer's base (today Turin or ISRO Bengaluru), with the similarity you give up.

Each place card shows the score of every parameter with the sensor behind it, on Earth and on the target, what holds in the field, what is partial and what breaks, the test window (snow-free months), and the campaign: the field site plus the smallest set of indoor facilities that close every gap. The campaign can be copied as a plain-text brief.

HOW IT WORKS

- Earth is split into H3 hexagons of about 253 km2 of bare ground. Oceans, vegetation, farmland and cities are masked out.

- We measure the same metrics on both bodies. Slope, roughness and crater density on the Moon are computed by us on the LRO LOLA 20 m DEM, with the same code and the same 30 m baseline we use on Earth (NASADEM, JAXA AW3D30). The other parameters are boulder cover, regolith grain size (a thermal-inertia proxy from MODIS land temperature), albedo, low-angle sunlight, surface density, rock type and ground ice. Mars and Aristarchus values come from the literature.

- Each parameter scores exp(-(D/0.1)^2), where D is the distance from the target value in Earth percentiles. The total is a weighted geometric mean with the weights of the chosen test, and a place is ranked only if at least 80% of the weight has data.

- The global screen runs at 500 m. Candidates and known sites get exact 30 m values, and a gradient-boosting model calibrates 500 m to 30 m everywhere else, with its error declared.

- Validation: real test sites rank near the top for the tests they are actually used for. SP Crater reaches the 100th percentile for rover mobility (Haworth), Mojave the 96th for lidar landing (Malapert), Rogers Dry Lake and Mauna Kea the 95th, and Etna the 89th.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Faster site selection. Today two engineers spend about three weeks reading papers and going back to the same few sites (Etna, Arizona, the Canary Islands, Atacama). POLENTA produces the ranked shortlist in minutes, and one engineer checks it in about three days. On a real campaign we estimate 57 to 20 person-days to choose the site, and being in the field 4 to 8 weeks earlier.

- New places. 61 of our 90 best places (the top 5 for each of the 18 site and test pairs) lie outside every known test site and analog region. Some surprises: the Tibetan Plateau for Mars ground ice, natural fields of crater-like depressions in Patagonia for lunar landing sensors, and Montana for Gale-like rover terrain.

- Closer to home. For rover mobility on the Aristarchus Plateau, the best site within 3,000 km of Turin keeps 65% of the test in the field all year round, and the app names the facilities in Turin (ALTEC) and at partners that close the rest.

- Who it is for: the Turin space cluster first (Thales Alenia Space, ALTEC, Argotec, AIKO, Evolunar), then ESA, ASI, ISRO and ispace. Smaller teams and universities get a site search that today needs years of field experience. Next steps: a pilot on one real campaign with a Turin test team, more tests (EVA, drilling, cameras), a permits dossier, and finally a campaign quote in money, time and people before anyone commits.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It turns analog selection from "go where everyone goes" into a search over all the bare land on Earth, using the same definitions on the Moon and on Earth.

- It is honest about the analogy: every place shows what breaks, and the field site and the indoor facilities are planned together as one campaign.

- "Near you" makes the trade-off between similarity and distance explicit, so a team can choose a site it can actually reach.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Earth never reproduces 1/6 gravity, vacuum, electrostatic dust, the engine plume in vacuum or lunar agglutinates. These always go to indoor facilities.

- Data limits are stated in the app and in the repository. This is model output, not a site survey: 30 m terrain and roughly 1 km satellite data averaged over hexagons. Ground ice is a MODIS proxy, rock type is coarse (GLiM), and Antarctica is not covered.

- Practical constraints: the test window (snow-free months), protected areas (WDPA permit warning), distance from the customer's base, and data coverage. Every number traces back to a named sensor.

TOOLS

- NASA data: NASADEM; MODIS MOD44W, MOD13A3, MOD11A2, MCD43A3 and MOD10A2; VIIRS DNB; MERRA-2; LRO LOLA (PDS); NASA GIBS, Moon Trek and Viking MDIM imagery; NASA 3D Resources. Partner and open data: JAXA AW3D30, SoilGrids, GLiM, JRC Global Surface Water, WDPA.

- Pipeline: Python, Google Earth Engine, H3, NumPy, pandas, rasterio, SciPy, scikit-learn (gradient boosting), pvlib.

- App: JavaScript, React, Vite, MapLibre GL, deck.gl, three.js and h3-js, hosted on Vercel. The pitch deck is HTML, CSS and canvas, and the demo video was recorded with Playwright and ffmpeg.

- Code was written with AI assistance (Claude Code). Every number in the app and in the pitch comes from our pipeline output.
